query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has been focused on understanding their unique properties, such as high strength, ductility, and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. Studies have explored the effects of grain boundary structure, precipitation conditions, and deformation mechanisms on the mechanical properties of these alloys. Recently, there has been a shift towards investigating the temperature dependence of elastic and plastic deformation behavior, as well as the origin of age softening in refractory high-entropy alloys.
decision.unsolved: The exact mechanisms governing toughness degradation in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys remain unknown, and the relationship between grain boundary structure, precipitation conditions, and deformation mechanisms is not fully understood. Additionally, the long-term stability of refractory high-entropy alloys under potential service temperatures is still a topic of research.
decision.why: To further understand the mechanisms governing toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys, it is necessary to investigate the grain boundary structure and precipitation conditions at the atomic scale. Atom probe tomography is a powerful tool for characterizing the composition and structure of materials at the nanoscale, and can provide valuable insights into the relationships between grain boundary structure, precipitation conditions, and deformation mechanisms.
